segments.text: Put living cells under a microscope, and a camera sees almost nothing: they're nearly transparent.
segments.say: Put living cells under a microscope, and a camera sees almost nothing. They're nearly transparent.

segments.text: Yet the light that went through them changed a lot. Not in brightness, but in phase: the cells delayed it.
segments.say: Yet the light that went through them changed a lot. Not in brightness, but in phase: the cells delayed it.

segments.text: So how do you photograph something a camera can't see?
segments.say: So how do you photograph something, a camera can't see?

segments.text: That's the phase problem. Its solutions are holography and phase retrieval.
segments.say: That's the phase problem. Its solutions are holography, and phase retrieval.

segments.text: Remember: at each point, light is an arrow, a complex number. Its length is the amplitude, its angle the phase.
segments.say: Remember: at each point, light is an arrow, a complex number. Its length is the amplitude, and its angle is the phase.

segments.text: A cell slows light down slightly. Where it's thicker, the light falls further behind, so its arrow turns further.
segments.say: A cell slows light down slightly. Where it's thicker, the light falls further behind, so its arrow turns further.

segments.text: But a camera can't record arrows. It records brightness, the squared length |U|², and throws every angle away.
segments.say: But a camera can't record arrows. It records brightness, the squared length, and throws every angle away.

segments.text: Why not measure the angle? Every arrow spins: green light oscillates 600 trillion times a second, far too fast for any detector.
segments.say: Why not measure the angle? Every arrow spins: green light oscillates six hundred trillion times a second, far too fast for any detector.

segments.text: So for a transparent object, all the information sits in the phase, the very part the camera loses.
segments.say: So for a transparent object, all the information sits in the phase, the very part the camera loses.

segments.text: Dennis Gabor's idea, in 1948: add a known reference wave, R. It spins in step with U, so the angle between them holds still.
segments.say: Dennis Gah-bor's idea, in nineteen forty-eight: add a known reference wave, R. It spins in step with U, so the angle between them holds still.

segments.text: The camera sees the length of the sum, U + R. Change U's phase, and that length grows and shrinks.
segments.say: The camera sees the length of the sum, U plus R. Change U's phase, and that length grows and shrinks.

segments.text: The phase is now written in brightness.
segments.say: The phase is now written in brightness.

segments.text: Expanding the square gives four terms. The two cross terms, UR* and U*R, contain U itself, phase and all.
segments.say: Expanding the square gives four terms. The two cross terms, U R star, and U star R, contain U itself, phase and all.

segments.text: With the reference straight on, as in Gabor's setup, all four terms pile up in one place, and the twin, U*, spoils the picture.
segments.say: With the reference straight on, as in Gah-bor's setup, all four terms pile up in one place, and the twin, U star, spoils the picture.

segments.text: In 1962, Leith and Upatnieks tilted the reference. Now the camera records fine stripes, called fringes.
segments.say: In nineteen sixty-two, Leith and Oo-pat-nieks tilted the reference. Now the camera records fine stripes, called fringes.

segments.text: A tilt is a shift in spatial frequency. So in the spectrum, UR* slides to one side, and its twin to the other.
segments.say: A tilt is a shift in spatial frequency. So in the spectrum, U R star slides to one side, and its twin to the other.

segments.text: Here's a computed off-axis hologram of our cells. Take its Fourier transform, and three islands appear.
segments.say: Here's a computed off-axis hologram of our cells. Take its Fourier transform, and three islands appear.

segments.text: The middle island holds |U|² and |R|². On either side sits one cross term: UR*, and its twin.
segments.say: The middle island holds U squared and R squared. On either side sits one cross term: U R star, and its twin.

segments.text: They mustn't overlap. The middle one is twice as wide, so the tilt's frequency must be at least three times the object's bandwidth.
segments.say: They mustn't overlap. The middle one is twice as wide, so the tilt's frequency must be at least three times the object's bandwidth.

segments.text: Now crop one island, move it to the centre, and transform back.
segments.say: Now crop one island, move it to the centre, and transform back.

segments.text: Out comes the full complex field: brightness shows amplitude, and colour shows phase.
segments.say: Out comes the full complex field: brightness shows amplitude, and colour shows phase.

segments.text: We recorded this hologram out of focus. But with the whole field in hand, the angular spectrum method from episode one can propagate it anywhere.
segments.say: We recorded this hologram out of focus. But with the whole field in hand, the angular spectrum method from episode one can propagate it anywhere.

segments.text: Sweep the distance, and the cells snap into focus, long after the picture was taken.
segments.say: Sweep the distance, and the cells snap into focus, long after the picture was taken.

segments.text: What if there's no reference, only brightness? Then you lean on what you already know.
segments.say: What if there's no reference, only brightness? Then you lean on what you already know.

segments.text: Here, light passes through a window of known shape, and the sample is transparent. So in this plane, every arrow's length is known.
segments.say: Here, light passes through a window of known shape, and the sample is transparent. So in this plane, every arrow's length is known.

segments.text: A lens shows the far field, and a camera there gives its lengths too. Lengths in both planes, angles in neither.
segments.say: A lens shows the far field, and a camera there gives its lengths too. Lengths in both planes, angles in neither.

segments.text: The Gerchberg–Saxton algorithm starts from random angles and goes back and forth with Fourier transforms.
segments.say: The Gherchberg Saxton algorithm starts from random angles, and goes back and forth with Fourier transforms.

segments.text: In each plane, it keeps the angles, but swaps in the lengths it knows.
segments.say: In each plane, it keeps the angles, but swaps in the lengths it knows.

segments.text: Each swap puts the guess on one constraint. Bouncing between them, it homes in on a field that satisfies both.
segments.say: Each swap puts the guess on one constraint. Bouncing between them, it homes in on a field that satisfies both.

segments.text: Watch the error fall, as the cells emerge from the noise.
segments.say: Watch the error fall, as the cells emerge from the noise.

segments.text: The far field alone has blind spots: a shifted copy, a flipped twin, or a constant phase gives exactly the same brightness.
segments.say: The far field alone has blind spots: a shifted copy, a flipped twin, or a constant phase, gives exactly the same brightness.

segments.text: Our lopsided window rules out the first two. More diverse data helps too: several distances, or the overlapping scans of ptychography.
segments.say: Our lopsided window rules out the first two. More diverse data helps too: several distances, or the overlapping scans of tie-kography.

segments.text: Now run it backwards. Instead of measuring a far field, ask for one: say, a λ.
segments.say: Now run it backwards. Instead of measuring a far field, ask for one: say, a lambda.

segments.text: The mask can only change phase, like a liquid-crystal screen or an etched glass plate. Same loop, with the target in place of the measurement.
segments.say: The mask can only change phase, like a liquid crystal screen, or an etched glass plate. Same loop, with the target in place of the measurement.

segments.text: Watch the mask's phase scramble, and the far field snap into the target.
segments.say: Watch the mask's phase scramble, and the far field snap into the target.

segments.text: The grain is speckle. The target fixes only brightness, so the far-field phase comes out random, and nearby points interfere with each other, as in episode four.
segments.say: The grain is speckle. The target fixes only brightness, so the far field phase comes out random, and nearby points interfere with each other, as in episode four.

segments.text: Modern designs often use gradient descent instead, which we'll meet in episode ten.
segments.say: Modern designs often use gradient descent instead, which we'll meet in episode ten.

segments.text: On a computer, each idea is just a few lines.
segments.say: On a computer, each idea is just a few lines.

segments.text: Holography: FFT the hologram, crop the island, inverse FFT, then refocus with the angular spectrum method.
segments.say: Holography: F F T the hologram, crop the island, inverse F F T, then refocus with the angular spectrum method.

segments.text: Retrieval and design: a loop of FFTs that swaps in what you know.
segments.say: Retrieval and design: a loop of F F Ts that swaps in what you know.

segments.text: Two pitfalls. Every fringe needs at least two pixels, or the island runs off the edge of the spectrum and wraps around.
segments.say: Two pitfalls. Every fringe needs at least two pixels, or the island runs off the edge of the spectrum, and wraps around.

segments.text: So off-axis holography spends part of the camera's pixels on fringes.
segments.say: So off-axis holography spends part of the camera's pixels on fringes.

segments.text: And Gerchberg–Saxton can stall. Restart it from new random angles, or switch to gradients.
segments.say: And Gherchberg Saxton can stall. Restart it from new random angles, or switch to gradients.

segments.text: Cameras lose phase. Interference writes it into fringes, and constraints let a computer recover it, or design it.
segments.say: Cameras lose phase. Interference writes it into fringes, and constraints let a computer recover it, or design it.

segments.text: Where does it break? Holography needs steady, coherent light, and retrieval needs diverse data.
segments.say: Where does it break? Holography needs steady, coherent light, and retrieval needs diverse data.
